title: Vector
body:
A **vector** is a quantity with both magnitude and direction, drawn as an arrow. That is the
first-year picture and it is enough for $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$. The version that
scales is the algebraic one: **a vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers**, an element of
$\mathbb{R}^n$, and the arrow is just what the list looks like when $n \leq 3$.

$$
\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

Written as a **column** by default, per the convention set out in [[Matrix Multiplication]], so
that $A\mathbf{v}$ typechecks. A vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an $n \times 1$ [[Matrix]], and
nothing about matrix algebra needs a special case for it.

Once you stop insisting on the arrow, $n$ stops being limited to $3$. A point in $\mathbb{R}^{784}$
is a $28 \times 28$ greyscale image flattened out, and that is exactly how [[MACHINE LEARNING]]
uses this material.

## Arithmetic

**Addition is componentwise**, and geometrically it is tip-to-tail: walk along $\mathbf{u}$,
then along $\mathbf{v}$, and $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ is the arrow from where you started to
where you ended.

**Scalar multiplication** stretches: $c\mathbf{v}$ has the same direction and $|c|$ times the
length, and flips direction if $c < 0$.

$$
\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 + v_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n + v_n \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
c\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} cv_1 \\ \vdots \\ cv_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

**These two operations are the entire structure.** Everything in [[Vector Space]] is the
observation that many things you would not call arrows support exactly these two operations and
therefore behave identically.

## Norm

The **norm** (length, magnitude) of $\mathbf{v}$ is

$$
\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots + v_n^2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}}
$$

which is Pythagoras, run in $n$ dimensions instead of two. Properties: $\|\mathbf{v}\| \geq 0$
with equality only for the zero vector, $\|c\mathbf{v}\| = |c|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|$, and the
triangle inequality $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\| + \|\mathbf{v}\|$ (the
direct route is never longer than the detour).

**Distance** between two points is the norm of their difference:
$d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|$.

A **unit vector** has norm $1$. Normalising means dividing by the norm,
$\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}/\|\mathbf{v}\|$, which keeps direction and throws away
magnitude. Useful whenever you care which way something points and not how far.

The one written above is the Euclidean norm, sometimes $\|\cdot\|_2$. Other norms exist and
matter later: $\|\cdot\|_1$ sums absolute values, $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ takes the largest
component. They become loss functions in [[MACHINE LEARNING]], which is [[Vector Norm]]'s
material in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303).

## The standard basis

In $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\mathbf{i} = (1,0,0)$, $\mathbf{j} = (0,1,0)$, $\mathbf{k} = (0,0,1)$, and
every vector is $v_1\mathbf{i} + v_2\mathbf{j} + v_3\mathbf{k}$. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ these are
written $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$. **A vector's components are already its
coordinates in this basis**, which is so convenient it is easy to forget it is a choice. See
[[Basis]] for what happens when you make a different one.

- [[Vector Space]]: the abstraction over these two operations

  is where [[Gradient]], [[Curl]], and [[Divergence]] live
- [[Matrix Multiplication]]: $A\mathbf{v}$ is how a matrix acts on a vector
